Schema: docs/content/QUESTION_SCHEMA.md; writing rules: docs/content/EXAM_STYLE_V2.md and .claude/agents/crisc-standards-auditor.md. Not affiliated with or endorsed by ISACA®. questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Near miss after a fix
questions.question: A nurse at a regional hospital catches a lab result routed to the wrong patient's chart, and the lab fixes the routing rule the same day. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Link the event to its risk scenario and reassess the rating
options.B: Close the incident with the scenario's risk rating unchanged
options.C: Have the lab manager assess a second check on results
options.D: Report the near miss to the board for urgent review

questions.key_concept: Near misses are likelihood evidence; after any event, reassess the linked risk scenario before anyone chooses new controls.
questions.pre_read: Notice what happened, what was lost and what has already been fixed.
questions.correct_explanation: A near miss is likelihood evidence: it shows the misrouting scenario can happen and that a nurse was the last barrier. Once the fault is contained, the risk practitioner links the event to its scenario and reassesses likelihood and impact, so the risk owner can decide whether the fix is enough. Weighing a second check may help, but it studies a control before the risk itself is reassessed.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the fault is fixed. But fixing the cause closes the ticket, not the risk; the near miss is new evidence the rating must reflect.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since a second check could prevent repeats. But it studies a control before the risk is reassessed, and choosing the response belongs to the risk owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because patient safety is serious. But the board sets appetite; one near miss is first analyzed and reported through the risk owner, not escalated unassessed.

tips: Eliminate: B closes the incident while leaving the rating blind to new evidence, and D sends one unassessed near miss to the board, which sets appetite rather than reviewing single events.
Final two: A beats C because the near miss must first update the scenario's rating; only then can the risk owner judge whether another control is worth it.
Exam cue: once an incident or near miss is contained, the first risk move is to update the scenario and its rating, even when the fault is already fixed.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 APO12.01 (Collect Data); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Maintaining the Risk Assessment)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A1.1 Loss Events, Incidents and Near Misses (near misses are likelihood evidence; closing the incident is not closing the risk). Original hospital lab-routing scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D2 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): B now keeps the rating instead of closing a risk; lens word 'assess' added to runner-up C; options trimmed of reasons; containment caveat in the exam cue; candidate renamed risk practitioner; neutral pre_read.

questions.subtopic: 2A1 Risk events. Gradual AI performance change
questions.question: Over six months, a bank's loan-triage AI model has gradually routed more sound applications to manual review, raising handling costs, but no incident was logged. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Monitor the scenario's manual review rate with a new KRI
options.B: Have the data science team retrain the model on recent loans
options.C: Log the drift as a data science tuning task to assess
options.D: Log the trend as a risk event and reassess the AI scenario

questions.key_concept: Model drift is a risk event; record it against the AI risk scenario and reassess before anyone chooses a fix.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has changed, over what period, and what records exist so far.
questions.correct_explanation: Drift is a risk event even when nothing fails: rising manual review is a real cost that builds gradually. The risk practitioner first logs it against the AI triage scenario and reassesses likelihood and impact, so the business owner can decide on a response. Retraining may well be the answer, but it is a treatment the owner chooses after analysis, with the data science team acting as control owner.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a KRI tracks the trend. But six months of drift is already evidence; the scenario is reassessed first, and KRI thresholds come from that assessment.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, because retraining often fixes drift. But it acts before the risk is assessed, and the business owner, not the risk practitioner, chooses the treatment.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because data scientists tune models. But filing drift as backlog work keeps a business risk away from its owner and out of the register.

tips: Eliminate: A sets up monitoring for a trend that already needs assessing, and C files drift as tuning work, keeping a business risk out of the register.
Final two: D beats B because the drift must be logged and assessed first; retraining is a treatment the business owner chooses after that analysis.
Exam cue: AI bias and drift are risk events with a business owner. Record and assess them like any other event before anyone fixes the model.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-1 (AI RMF 1.0) MEASURE 2.4 (the functionality and behavior of the AI system are monitored when in production); COBIT 2019 APO12.01 (Collect Data)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A1.3 AI Risk Events: Bias and Model Drift (drift builds gradually, is logged against an AI scenario with a business owner, and is assessed before retraining). Original bank loan-triage scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D2 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): strawman 'wait for a loss' replaced by a KRI distractor; lens words 'scenario' and 'assess' added to distractors; re-lettered (key B to D); candidate renamed risk practitioner; neutral pre_read. Cross-domain gate 31 Oct 2026: setting moved from an insurer to a bank so it no longer mirrors crisc_d3_017's insurer drift item.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. Threat source classification
questions.question: A risk analyst at a logistics firm records a scenario in which a database administrator runs a cleanup script on production instead of test. Which threat source type BEST fits under NIST SP 800-30?

options.A: Adversarial source: a privileged insider threat
options.B: Structural source: a database software failure
options.C: Accidental source: a privileged user's error
options.D: Environmental source: an infrastructure failure

questions.key_concept: NIST SP 800-30 classes everyday errors by staff, including privileged administrators, as accidental threat sources, separate from adversarial insiders.
questions.pre_read: Notice who acted, what they intended and what actually failed.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-30 Table D-2 classes erroneous actions by people doing their everyday jobs, including privileged users and administrators, as accidental threat sources. The administrator had no intent to harm; they ran the right script on the wrong system. Adversarial sources, privileged insiders included, act on purpose, so intent rather than access level separates the two. That matters, because likelihood for accidents comes from error history, not adversary capability.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice, since privileged insiders appear under adversarial sources. But adversarial means intent to harm; an administrator's honest mistake is accidental.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a database is software. But structural sources are equipment or software failing on their own; here the software worked and a person erred.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because production infrastructure was harmed. But environmental sources are natural disasters and outside infrastructure outages, not actions by the enterprise's staff.

tips: Eliminate: B needs equipment or software to fail on its own, and D covers disasters and outside infrastructure outages; here a person ran a script.
Final two: C beats A because the taxonomy separates sources by intent. Privileged insiders are adversarial only when they mean harm; an administrator's honest error is accidental.
Exam cue: classify a threat source by intent and cause, not by access level. Errors by staff doing their jobs are accidental, whatever their privileges.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Appendix D Table D-2 (Taxonomy of Threat Sources: adversarial, accidental, structural and environmental)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A2.1 Threat Sources and Threat Events (the four NIST SP 800-30 source types; intent separates adversarial from accidental). Original logistics database scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D2 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): options rewritten as parallel classifications without 'because' tails; D no longer invents an outage; neutral pre_read.

questions.subtopic: 2A2 Threat modeling and threat landscape. New AI threat intelligence
questions.question: A sector sharing group warns that applicants hide instructions in resumes to manipulate AI screening tools, and a recruitment firm's assistant summarizes uploaded resumes. What should the firm's risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Suspend resume uploads until the security team tests the assistant
options.B: Record a prompt injection risk for the assistant and assess it
options.C: Rely on existing email and web filters to block the instructions
options.D: Assess the alert as low likelihood for a firm not yet attacked

questions.key_concept: New AI threats such as indirect prompt injection are first recorded and assessed as scenarios with the business owner, before treatment.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the attack text would enter the system and who relies on the service.
questions.correct_explanation: Threat intelligence is an input to analysis, not a decision. The risk practitioner first records an indirect prompt injection risk for the screening assistant and assesses its likelihood and impact with the service owner, who then chooses the response. Suspending uploads might prove sensible, but deciding on it before analysis puts treatment ahead of assessment and takes the call from the owner, who must also weigh hiring delays.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice, since suspension closes the attack path. But it chooses a treatment before the risk is assessed, and that decision belongs to the service owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because filters screen content. But hidden instructions are ordinary text in approved documents; email and web filters cannot tell them from normal resume content.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because no attack has happened here. But credible intelligence about the same kind of tool raises likelihood; a quiet internal history does not mean low risk.

tips: Eliminate: C expects perimeter filters to spot instructions that arrive as ordinary text, and D rates likelihood low despite credible sector intelligence.
Final two: B beats A because a new threat is first assessed with its owner; suspending uploads is a treatment the owner chooses afterward.
Exam cue: when intelligence reports a new AI threat, record and assess the risk with its business owner before anyone switches features off.
questions.framework_ref: NIST AI 100-2 E2025 Section 3.4 (Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks and Mitigations); ISACA Glossary (prompt injection); NIST CSF 2.0 ID.RA-02 (cyber threat intelligence is received from information sharing forums and sources)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A2.3 AI-Specific Threats and 2A2.2 Threat Intelligence and Threat Modeling (intelligence is an input to scenario analysis; indirect injection arrives through content the model reads). Original recruitment-screening scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D2 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): key no longer the only option with 'owner' or 'scenario'; distractor C now 'assesses' the wrong thing; reason tails removed; re-lettered (key D to B); candidate renamed risk practitioner; neutral pre_read.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Severity scores in the register
questions.question: A bank's vulnerability team proposes copying each finding's CVSS Base score straight into the risk register as its risk rating. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Use the score as one input beside asset impact and exposure
options.B: Accept the proposal as a consistent industry-standard rating
options.C: Use each finding's CVSS-BTE score as its register risk rating
options.D: Rate each finding scored above 7.0 as a high register risk

questions.key_concept: A CVSS score is a severity input; a risk rating also needs the asset's business impact, its exposure and the likelihood of exploitation.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a CVSS score measures and what a register rating is used to decide.
questions.correct_explanation: A CVSS score, even fully adjusted, measures the technical severity of a flaw, and FIRST describes it as one input to risk assessment. Risk also depends on what the asset supports, how reachable it is and the business impact of exploitation, so the risk practitioner uses the score as one input to the scenario rating. Switching to CVSS-BTE improves the input, but it is still a severity score, not a business risk rating.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because CVSS is widely used and consistent. But a standard severity score still describes the flaw, not the business harm if the asset is exploited.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since threat and environmental metrics add context. But even CVSS-BTE stays a severity score; the rating still needs the business impact of exploitation.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because a threshold looks consistent. But a fixed cutoff ranks findings by severity alone, with no view of which business process each asset supports.

tips: Eliminate: B treats a standard severity score as business risk, and D sets register ratings by a severity cutoff with no view of what each asset supports.
Final two: A beats C because threat and environmental metrics refine severity, but business impact still has to be combined with the score to rate risk.
Exam cue: CVSS rates the flaw, not the risk. Expect the key to combine the score with asset value, exposure and business impact.
questions.framework_ref: FIRST Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 Specification Document Section 1 (Introduction); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Risk Models: threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A3.2 CVSS as a Severity Input (CVSS is severity, one input to risk; CVSS-BTE refines but does not replace business impact). Original bank vulnerability-team scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D2 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): reason tails removed and option lengths evened; candidate renamed risk practitioner; neutral pre_read.

questions.subtopic: 2A3 Vulnerability management. Control test finding
questions.question: Control tests at a hospital find pharmacists approve their own dosage-limit changes, which scans missed; on night shifts only one pharmacist is on duty. How should the risk practitioner BEST handle this finding?

options.A: Pass it to internal audit to track as a compliance issue
options.B: Rate the scenario low on the strength of clean system scans
options.C: Log it as a vulnerability in the medication error scenario
options.D: Have the pharmacy manager remove the self-approval right

questions.key_concept: Control deficiencies are vulnerabilities; record them against the affected risk scenarios and re-rate before treatment is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice where the weakness sits and what each obvious fix would cost on night shifts.
questions.correct_explanation: A control deficiency is a vulnerability: self-approval of dosage limits weakens protection against medication errors just as a missing patch weakens a server. The risk practitioner records it in the medication error scenario, re-rates it and, given the safety impact, takes it to the risk owner the same day. Removing the right looks obvious, but with one pharmacist on nights it could block urgent changes, a trade-off the owner must weigh.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because control test results often reach audit. But the weakness changes a business risk now; tracking it only as compliance keeps it out of the risk register.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the scans are clean. But scanners find technical flaws only; a self-approval right is a process weakness no scan can see.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice, since the gap looks urgent. But removal could stop the lone night pharmacist making urgent changes; the owner weighs that once the scenario is re-rated.

tips: Eliminate: A routes a live business risk to audit tracking instead of the register, and B trusts clean scans, which cannot find process weaknesses.

Final two: C beats D because the obvious fix carries its own night-shift safety cost; re-rating the scenario lets the risk owner weigh removal against options such as a next-morning independent review.
Exam cue: a failed or missing control is a vulnerability. Record it against the scenarios it weakens before anyone picks the fix.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (vulnerability); NIST IR 8286A Rev. 1 Section 2.2.3 (Vulnerability Identification)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A3.1 Vulnerabilities in People, Process and Technology (a control deficiency is a vulnerability; scanners miss process weaknesses). Original hospital pharmacy scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D2 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): HARD ERROR fix: stem now holds the deciding fact (one night pharmacist, so removal has its own safety cost) and asks how to 'handle', not 'treat'; key reworded; C without a reason tail; re-lettered (key B to C); candidate renamed risk practitioner.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Generic register entry
questions.question: A university's risk register lists 'cyberattack' as one high-rated scenario with no further detail, and owners cannot agree on controls. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Raise the scenario's rating to very high in the register
options.B: Ask IT to list every control that reduces cyberattack risk
options.C: Split it into specific scenarios with actor, asset and impact
options.D: Run a tabletop exercise on the scenario with business owners

questions.key_concept: A risk scenario must name the actor, event, asset, timing and consequence; generic entries cannot be rated, owned or linked to controls.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the register entry actually says and why the owners are stuck.
questions.correct_explanation: A scenario as broad as 'cyberattack' cannot be rated or tied to controls, which is why owners disagree. The risk practitioner first splits it into specific scenarios, each naming the actor, the asset affected and the business impact, so each one can be rated and owned. A tabletop exercise is valuable later, but exercising a vague scenario produces a vague discussion; specificity comes first.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because a higher rating gets attention. But re-rating a vague entry adds no information; it still cannot be tied to controls or owners.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because controls are what owners argue about. But a control list for a vague threat cannot show which controls matter for which assets.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice, since exercises test scenarios with the business. But a scenario this vague gives the exercise nothing concrete to test; define specific scenarios first.

tips: Eliminate: A re-rates an entry too vague to rate, and B lists controls before the scenario shows which assets and events they must address.
Final two: C beats D because a tabletop exercise needs a concrete scenario to test; splitting the generic entry into specific scenarios has to come first.
Exam cue: when owners cannot agree on a risk, check whether the scenario is specific: actor, event, asset, time and consequence.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (risk scenario); NIST IR 8286A Rev. 1 Section 2.2.5 (Recording Identified Risks: risk scenarios in cause-and-effect form)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2A4.1 Anatomy of a Risk Scenario (actor, event, asset, time, consequence; generic scenarios cannot be rated or owned). Original university register scenario written for KaiSip; no ISACA Review Manual, QAE, practice quiz or prep-bank text used. CRISC D2 pilot batch, 30 Oct 2026. Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): purpose tail removed from A; lens word 'scenario' now in distractors; candidate renamed risk practitioner; neutral pre_read.

questions.subtopic: 2A4 Risk scenario development and evaluation. Exercise finding
questions.question: At a retailer's tabletop exercise, store operations leaders say the top risk scenario misses that card payments fail when the loyalty service is down. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Revise the scenario with store operations and re-rate it
options.B: Keep the scenario as written by the risk team's experts
options.C: Ask the IT director to remove the loyalty service dependency
options.D: Note the comment in the exercise minutes for later review

questions.key_concept: Tabletop findings and business-owner input revise scenarios and the register before any treatment is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice who raised the gap and what they know about the business that others may not.
questions.correct_explanation: Tabletop exercises exist to expose gaps like this one, and the people who run the business know its dependencies best. The risk practitioner revises the scenario with store operations and re-rates it, updating the register so the new dependency is rated and owned. Asking IT to remove the dependency jumps to a fix before the revised scenario is assessed, and the risk owner, not the practitioner, chooses the response.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the risk team built the scenario carefully. But business leaders know the operational dependencies; a scenario they show to be incomplete must change.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since the dependency causes the harm. But it orders a fix before the revised scenario is assessed, and the response belongs to the risk owner.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the minutes capture it. But a finding that lives only in minutes is easily lost; it must become a register update with an owner.

tips: Eliminate: B overrides the business leaders who know the dependency, and D leaves an exercise finding in minutes rather than turning it into a tracked register update.
Final two: A beats C because the gap first updates the scenario and its rating; removing the dependency is a response the risk owner may choose afterward.
Exam cue: a tabletop finding should change the scenario and the register, with an owner. Look for the option that turns the gap into a tracked update.
questions.framework_ref: NIST CSF 2.0 ID.IM-02 (improvements are identified from security tests and exercises, including those done in coordination with suppliers and relevant third parties); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.3 (Analysis Approaches: threat-oriented, asset/impact-oriented and vulnerability-oriented)

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Starting a new assessment
questions.question: Before a new warehouse robotics system goes live, a logistics firm's COO asks the risk practitioner for a risk assessment. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Identify threats and vulnerabilities in the robotics system
options.B: Agree the purpose, scope and rating criteria with the COO
options.C: Request the vendor's security test results for the robots
options.D: Weigh the system's risk against appetite for the launch

questions.key_concept: A risk assessment begins by agreeing purpose, scope, assumptions and rating criteria, before identifying threats or rating risk.
questions.pre_read: Notice how much of the request has been defined so far.
questions.correct_explanation: NIST SP 800-30 starts every assessment with preparation: the purpose, the scope, the assumptions and the risk criteria. Without them the risk practitioner cannot tell which threats matter or how to rate them, and the COO may get answers to the wrong question. Identifying threats and vulnerabilities is the core of the work, but it belongs to the conduct step, after scope and criteria are agreed.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice, since threats and vulnerabilities are central. But without an agreed scope and criteria, the team cannot tell which ones matter or how to rate them.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because vendor tests are useful evidence. But they are one information source for the conduct step, not a substitute for preparing the assessment.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because appetite drives the launch decision. But risk cannot be compared with appetite before it is identified and analyzed; evaluation comes last.

tips: Eliminate: C treats one vendor input as the start of the assessment, and D compares risk with appetite before any risk has been analyzed.
Final two: B beats A because preparation comes before the conduct step; scope and criteria decide which threats and vulnerabilities are worth listing and how to rate them.
Exam cue: for the FIRST step of a new assessment, look for purpose, scope, context or criteria before any threat list or rating.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.1 (Preparing for the Risk Assessment: purpose, scope, assumptions, information sources and risk model)

Review fixes 30 Oct 2026 (blind test and standards audit): re-lettered (key A to B); candidate renamed risk practitioner; neutral pre_read.

questions.subtopic: 2B1 Risk assessment concepts and standards. Change after approval
questions.question: Eight months after a bank approved its risk assessment of a card-processing provider, the provider moves processing to a new subcontractor. What should the bank's risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Reassess the provider at the next scheduled annual review
options.B: Update the assessment for the change and brief the risk owner
options.C: Ask the risk owner to add a subcontractor clause to the contract
options.D: Discard the old assessment and start a new one from scratch

questions.key_concept: Risk assessments are maintained: a material change triggers an update and a briefing to the owner before new treatment is chosen.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has changed since the assessment was approved, and what has not.
questions.correct_explanation: An assessment stays live. The maintain step in NIST SP 800-30 monitors risk factors and updates the assessment when they change, and a new subcontractor changes who handles cardholder data. The risk practitioner updates the affected parts and briefs the risk owner, who decides on any response. A contract clause may well follow, but asking for one now treats a risk that has not yet been reassessed.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because reviews run on a cycle. But a material change to who processes the data triggers reassessment now, not at the next annual date.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since a subcontractor clause is a common fix. But it picks a treatment before the changed risk is reassessed; the owner should choose with the update in hand.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the old view is out of date. But most of the assessment still holds; maintaining it means updating the affected parts, not repeating all the work.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for the calendar despite a material change, and D repeats the whole assessment when only the changed factors need updating.
Final two: B beats C because the changed risk is reassessed and reported first; a contract clause is one response the owner may choose after seeing the update.
Exam cue: a significant change to a system, supplier or threat triggers an update to the assessment now, followed by communication to the risk owner.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.4 (Maintaining the Risk Assessment); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 3.3 (Communicating and Sharing Risk Assessment Information)

questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). BIA and risk assessment
questions.question: A city council's continuity manager argues that the new BIA already ranks the council's top risks, so no separate risk assessment is needed. What is the PRIMARY flaw in this view?

options.A: A BIA does not identify which processes are critical
options.B: A BIA studies threats but not the vulnerabilities they exploit
options.C: A BIA leaves recovery objectives for IT to set alone
options.D: A BIA assumes the disruption occurs and ignores likelihood

questions.key_concept: A BIA measures impact over time and ignores likelihood, so it complements a risk assessment but cannot replace it.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a BIA produces and what a ranking of risks requires.
questions.correct_explanation: A BIA measures how harm grows over time if a process stops, assuming the disruption happens. It never estimates how likely each disruption is, so it cannot rank risks on its own; a risk assessment combines likelihood with impact, using the BIA's impact data. The idea that a BIA studies threats is the runner-up, but a BIA examines neither threats nor vulnerabilities; it starts from the outage.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because criticality sounds like risk. But identifying critical processes is the BIA's main output; the missing piece is how likely each disruption is.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, since threats and vulnerabilities drive risk. But a BIA examines neither; it starts from the outage and measures impact, leaving likelihood unassessed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because recovery objectives sound technical. But a BIA gathers them from business owners; the gap in this view is likelihood, not who sets objectives.

tips: Eliminate: A denies the BIA's core output, critical processes, and C misplaces who sets recovery objectives, which a BIA gathers from business owners.
Final two: D beats B because a BIA does not study threats at all; it starts from the disruption, so the missing dimension for ranking risk is likelihood.
Exam cue: a BIA is impact over time, assuming the event happens. A risk assessment is likelihood and impact together. Neither replaces the other.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Glossary (business impact analysis); ISACA Glossary (risk)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: notes 2B2.1 BIA Purpose, Dependencies and AI Systems (a BIA assumes the disruption and ignores likelihood; it is not a risk assessment). questions.subtopic: 2B2 Business impact analysis (BIA). Recovery objective for an AI service
questions.question: A hospital's IT team sets a 48-hour RTO for its AI sepsis-alert service because that matches the vendor's standard restore time. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Accept the RTO based on the vendor's stated recovery capability
options.B: Ask IT to buy the vendor's faster recovery tier immediately
options.C: Set a matching 48-hour RPO for the sepsis-alert service data
options.D: Ask clinical leads how long care can safely run without alerts

questions.key_concept: RTO and RPO are set by business owners from BIA results, AI services included, not by IT or vendor capability.
questions.pre_read: Notice who set the RTO and what it was based on.
questions.correct_explanation: Recovery objectives come from the business through the BIA, not from what a vendor offers. The risk practitioner first asks the clinical leads how long care can run safely without sepsis alerts, which sets the tolerance the RTO must fit within. Buying a faster tier might follow, but spending before the business tolerance is known could buy too little recovery, or far too much.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the vendor knows its platform. But a vendor's restore time shows what is offered, not how long clinicians can work safely without alerts.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, since faster recovery looks safer. But it commits money before the business tolerance is known; the clinical leads' answer decides what recovery is needed.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because matching numbers look tidy. But RPO measures tolerable data loss, not restore time; it is set separately, from how much data the process can afford to lose.

tips: Eliminate: A lets the vendor's offer set the objective, and C confuses RPO, which measures tolerable data loss, with RTO, which measures restore time.
Final two: D beats B because the business tolerance must be known before recovery is bought; the clinical leads' answer sets what the RTO must achieve.
Exam cue: when IT or a vendor sets an RTO or RPO, the first move is to get the process owner's tolerance through the BIA.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Entry status after approval
questions.question: A retailer's risk register shows payment page skimming as closed because a script-integrity tool was approved last week, with deployment next quarter. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Leave it closed with the approved response recorded
options.B: Keep it closed but set a reminder to confirm deployment
options.C: Reopen it as in treatment, rated on current controls
options.D: Remove the entry until the new control is deployed

questions.key_concept: A register entry stays open, rated on current controls, until the planned response is implemented and shown to work.
questions.pre_read: Notice the dates: when the tool was approved and when it will be deployed.
questions.correct_explanation: Register status must follow evidence. An approved tool that is not yet deployed reduces nothing, so the entry is reopened as in treatment and rated on the controls actually in place today. A reminder to confirm deployment is useful, but leaving the entry closed meanwhile tells decision makers the skimming risk is handled when it is not.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because approval is a real milestone. But an approved plan is not a working control; the risk stays at its current level until deployment.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, since it tracks deployment. But the closed status still misreports today's exposure for months; status must reflect what is in place.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the control is coming. But removing the entry erases a live risk, its owner and its history before any reduction has happened.

tips: Eliminate: A counts an approved plan as a working control, and D erases a live risk from the register before any control exists.
Final two: C beats B because the register must show today's true status; a reminder tracks the rollout but leaves decision makers misled until deployment.
Exam cue: register status follows evidence. Planned or approved controls never close an entry or lower its current rating.

questions.subtopic: 2B3 Risk register. Rolling up unit ratings
questions.question: Rolling up unit registers for the enterprise risk profile, a supermarket chain's risk practitioner finds four regions each rate the same shared ordering-platform outage as low. What is the BEST action?

options.A: Report the outage as low, matching every region's rating
options.B: Merge the entries into one group scenario rated on combined impact
options.C: Average the four regional ratings into one group rating
options.D: Escalate the outage scenario to the board as a hidden risk

questions.key_concept: Aggregation can turn several low local risks into one significant enterprise risk when units share an asset or weakness.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the four regions have in common and how each rating was set.
questions.correct_explanation: When units share one platform, a single outage hits all four regions at once, so four low ratings can hide a significant group exposure. The risk practitioner merges the entries into one group scenario and rates its combined impact on the enterprise scale before reporting it in the profile. Escalating straight to the board is the runner-up, but it reports a risk nobody has yet rated at group level.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because every region agrees. But each region rated only its own slice; one shared outage hits all four at once, so the combined impact is larger.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because averaging looks like normalization. But an average of four low ratings stays low and still misses the combined impact of one shared failure.
wrong_explanations.D: Closest choice, since the exposure may be significant. But it escalates before the combined risk is rated; the board needs an analyzed group rating to compare with appetite.

tips: Eliminate: A treats four local lows as a low group risk, and C averages the ratings, which keeps the shared outage's combined impact hidden.
Final two: B beats D because the combined risk must be rated at group level first; escalating an unrated concern gives the board nothing to compare with appetite.
Exam cue: when several units share one asset or weakness, aggregate their entries into one enterprise scenario and rate the combined impact.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Annualized loss calculation
questions.question: An e-commerce firm's checkout platform is valued at $600,000; each outage loses 25 percent of that value and happens about once every three years. What is the BEST estimate of the ALE?

options.A: About $50,000 a year
options.B: About $150,000 a year
options.C: About $450,000 a year
options.D: About $200,000 a year

questions.key_concept: ALE equals SLE times ARO, where SLE is asset value times exposure factor and ARO is the expected number of events per year.
questions.pre_read: Separate the loss from one outage from how often outages happen.
questions.correct_explanation: SLE is asset value times exposure factor: $600,000 times 0.25 is $150,000. An event once every three years gives an ARO of about 0.33. ALE is SLE times ARO, so about $50,000 a year. The runner-up, $150,000, is the SLE: the loss from a single outage before accounting for how rarely it happens. ALE is the figure to compare with a control's yearly cost.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: this is the SLE, the loss from one outage. It leaves out the annual rate of occurrence of one outage every three years.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting if the three years is multiplied in. But the ARO is one third a year, so the SLE is divided by three, not multiplied.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it divides by three. But it skips the 25 percent exposure factor, treating the whole platform value as lost in each outage.

tips: Eliminate: C multiplies by three when an event every three years gives an ARO of one third, and D skips the 25 percent exposure factor.
Final two: A beats B because B is the SLE for one outage; multiplying it by the ARO of one third gives the yearly expectation.
Exam cue: SLE equals asset value times exposure factor, ARO is events per year, and ALE equals SLE times ARO. Once every N years means an ARO of one over N.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286A Rev. 1 Section 2.2.4 (Determining Potential Impact: single loss expectancy and annualized loss expectancy)

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Funding a failover
questions.question: A clinic chain's records outage has an ALE of $80,000, and a $30,000-a-year failover would cut it to $20,000. What is the risk practitioner's BEST advice to the records owner?

options.A: Advise against it: its $30,000 cost exceeds the $20,000 residual ALE
options.B: Advise against it: five years of cost exceed the $80,000 ALE
options.C: Recommend it: it cuts the yearly expected loss by 75 percent
options.D: Recommend it: a $60,000 yearly loss reduction for a $30,000 cost

questions.key_concept: A control is cost-justified when the yearly ALE reduction exceeds its yearly cost; percentages and mismatched time periods mislead, and the risk owner decides.
questions.pre_read: Line up each figure with the period it covers before comparing them.
questions.correct_explanation: Cost-benefit compares the yearly cut in ALE with the control's yearly cost: $80,000 minus $20,000 is a $60,000 reduction against a $30,000 cost, a net benefit of $30,000 a year. The risk practitioner recommends the failover on that case, and the records owner decides. A 75 percent cut sounds persuasive, but a percentage alone cannot show whether the saving exceeds the cost.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because $30,000 is more than $20,000. But the residual ALE is what remains; the benefit is the $60,000 reduction, double the cost.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because a multi-year view looks prudent. But it sets five years of spending against one year of expected loss; compare both on a yearly basis.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since the cut is real. But a percentage ignores cost; a 75 percent cut could still cost more than the loss it removes.

tips: Eliminate: A compares cost with the residual ALE instead of the reduction, and B sets five years of cost against one year of expected loss.
Final two: D beats C because cost-benefit weighs the yearly loss reduction against the yearly cost; a percentage cut alone cannot show the control is worth buying.
Exam cue: control value is ALE before minus ALE after, compared with yearly cost. Then check who decides: the risk owner, not the practitioner.

questions.subtopic: 2B4 Risk analysis methodologies. Request for an exact figure
questions.question: A payments start-up's board asks for one exact ALE for fraud on a new product, but there is no loss history and only one expert's guess. What is the risk practitioner's BEST approach?

options.A: Report one exact ALE figure built from the expert's single guess
options.B: Give a loss range from calibrated estimates and state the uncertainty
options.C: Delay the analysis until three years of fraud loss data exist
options.D: Rate it high on the word scale until better loss data arrives

questions.key_concept: Quantitative results must match input quality; with thin data, give ranges and stated uncertainty rather than a falsely precise figure.
questions.pre_read: Notice how much data stands behind the number the board wants.
questions.correct_explanation: With no loss history and one guess, a single exact ALE would carry false precision and could mislead the board. The risk practitioner gives a loss range built from several calibrated expert estimates, states the uncertainty and assumptions, and shows how better data would narrow it. Reporting one figure meets the request literally, but NIST SP 800-30 warns that buried subjective inputs strip a quantitative result of its rigor.

wrong_explanations.A: Closest choice, since it gives the board what it asked for. But one figure from one guess looks precise without being reliable, so the board would decide with false confidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the data is thin. But decisions cannot wait years; ranges from calibrated estimates give usable analysis now, with the uncertainty made clear.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because missing data feels risky. But a rating must reflect estimated likelihood and impact; defaulting to high because data is thin distorts priorities.

tips: Eliminate: C withholds analysis the board needs now, and D rates the risk by its data gaps instead of by estimated likelihood and impact.
Final two: B beats A because a range with stated uncertainty is honest about thin data, while a single figure from one guess gives the board false precision.
Exam cue: when data is poor, prefer ranges, stated assumptions or qualitative ratings over exact-looking numbers. Precision must match the inputs.
questions.framework_ref: NIST IR 8286A Rev. 1 Section 2.3.1 (Selecting Risk Analysis Methodologies); NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Section 2.3.2 (Assessment Approaches: subjective inputs or high uncertainty lessen quantitative rigor)

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Rating compared with appetite
questions.question: A water utility's risk practitioner is preparing advice on whether its control system intrusion scenario needs more treatment. Which rating is MOST appropriate to compare with risk appetite?

options.A: Residual risk, counting only controls implemented and working
options.B: Residual risk projected once next year's planned controls go live
options.C: Inherent risk, before any of the utility's controls are counted
options.D: Whichever of the inherent and residual ratings is higher

questions.key_concept: Treatment decisions compare residual risk, crediting only implemented and working controls, with risk appetite.
questions.pre_read: Notice which controls exist today and which are only planned.
questions.correct_explanation: Treatment decisions compare the risk that remains after implemented, working controls with appetite; in ISACA terms this is also today's current risk. If it is within appetite, the owner can accept and monitor it; if above, more treatment is considered. A projection counting next year's planned controls is the runner-up, but it is a target, not today's exposure.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, since it is labeled residual risk. But planned controls reduce nothing yet; a projection is a target, and counting it understates today's exposure.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because inherent risk shows the full threat. But it leaves out controls already working, so comparing it with appetite overstates the need for treatment.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because it feels cautious. But the higher rating is always the inherent one, so this leaves out working controls and pushes treatment the evidence does not support.

tips: Eliminate: C leaves out controls that already work, overstating the need for treatment, and D in effect always picks the inherent rating.
Final two: A beats B because only implemented, working controls reduce risk today; a projection with planned controls is a target, not the exposure to compare with appetite.
Exam cue: compare residual risk, counting only working controls, with appetite. Inherent risk shows reliance on controls; it does not decide treatment.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Untested control credit
questions.question: A university's register rates research data theft as low residual risk because laptop encryption was installed two years ago, though it has never been tested. What should the risk practitioner do FIRST?

options.A: Keep the low rating on the owner's word that it is installed
options.B: Re-rate the scenario at its inherent level until it is tested
options.C: Ask IT for coverage reports showing the encryption is active
options.D: Recommend replacing the tool with a newer encryption product

questions.key_concept: Residual ratings credit controls only for demonstrated effectiveness; obtain evidence before keeping or changing the rating.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the low rating relies on and when that control was last checked.
questions.correct_explanation: A control earns credit in residual risk only for what evidence shows it does, and existence is not effectiveness. The risk practitioner first gets evidence from IT, the control owner, such as device coverage reports and recovery-key checks. Re-rating to inherent is the runner-up, but it discards the encryption without evidence and every other control too; inherent counts no controls at all. Facts first, then the rating.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because the owner vouches for it. But installed is not effective: encryption may be disabled or missing from devices, and only evidence earns a low rating.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice, since the current rating is unsupported. But inherent ignores every other control as well, and dropping credit without evidence is as unfounded as keeping it.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because newer tools sound stronger. But nobody yet knows whether the current tool is failing; replacing it before getting evidence treats an unanalyzed gap.

tips: Eliminate: A treats an installed tool as proven effective, and D replaces a control before anyone knows whether it is failing.
Final two: C beats B because the rating should follow evidence; dropping to inherent also discards every other control and is as unsupported as keeping the low rating.
Exam cue: when a rating relies on an untested control, the first step is evidence of design and operating effectiveness, then re-rating.

questions.subtopic: 2B5 Inherent and residual risk. Residual above appetite
questions.question: After two new controls, a city council's ransomware scenario still has residual risk above the appetite its elected council approved. What is the risk practitioner's BEST next step?

options.A: Sign off the residual risk once the two new controls are live
options.B: Report the large drop from inherent risk as an acceptable result
options.C: Ask IT, as control owner, to deploy a third control now
options.D: Present further treatment options and costs to the risk owner

questions.key_concept: When residual risk exceeds appetite, the practitioner presents costed treatment options and the risk owner chooses the response.
questions.pre_read: Notice where residual risk sits against appetite after the new controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Residual risk above appetite needs more treatment, but the choice belongs to the risk owner. The risk practitioner presents options, such as further mitigation, transfer or changing the activity, with their costs and target ratings, so the owner can decide. Asking IT to deploy a third control may end up as one of those options, but directing it skips the owner's decision and the cost-benefit comparison.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because real effort has been made. But risk above appetite needs more treatment or a decision by the level that set appetite; acceptance is never the practitioner's call.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because the risk did fall. But decisions compare residual risk with appetite, not with inherent risk; a large reduction can still leave risk above appetite.
wrong_explanations.C: Closest choice, since IT runs the controls. But it picks the treatment for the owner; options and costs go to the risk owner, who chooses the response.

tips: Eliminate: A has the practitioner sign off risk that exceeds appetite, and B judges success against inherent risk rather than against appetite.
Final two: D beats C because the risk owner chooses the treatment from costed options; directing IT to add a control takes that decision from the owner.
Exam cue: residual risk above appetite means more treatment, chosen by the risk owner from options the practitioner prepares. Watch for options where the practitioner decides.
